transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because my mind keeps going blank, and it’s been scaring me. It’s not just forgetting a word or walking into a room and forgetting why—I mean, I’ll be at work, looking at the road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle, things I’ve done for years, and suddenly I just… can’t remember the steps. Like my head goes empty right when I need it not to.

It happens at the worst times, when I’m supposed to know exactly what to do, and then I start trying to force myself to remember, but that almost makes it worse. I’ll stare at the paperwork or the sign, and it feels like everything I know is just out of reach. That’s really why I’m here. I don’t feel like I can keep brushing it off.
Do these blank moments seem to happen more often when you're under a lot of stress or pressure?

Yes… I think pressure makes it worse, or at least that’s when I notice it the most, because there’s no room to cover for it. Like if I’m just at home and my mind goes blank, I can pause or retrace what I was doing, but at work it’s different. I’ll be looking right at the road-closure forms, or I’ll have the stop-slow paddle in my hand, and it’s something I’ve done for years, like I should know it automatically, and suddenly I just can’t remember the steps.

And then because I know I’m supposed to act quickly and get it right, I start panicking inside and trying to force my brain to come back online, but it’s like the harder I try, the emptier it gets. It’s not just ordinary distraction. It feels like the information is there somewhere, but I can’t reach it when I need it.
Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed outside of these blank moments, in your daily life?

I’m… not completely sure how to answer that. I mean, I know I get wound up when those blank moments happen, because it feels like I’m going to mess something up or look incompetent, especially at work. But outside of that, in just normal daily life, I don’t know if I’d call it anxious exactly.

I do feel overwhelmed sometimes, but I haven’t really separated it out in my head, if that makes sense. Like I’ll be going through the day and I know I’m tense, or I feel like I have too much to keep track of, but I don’t always notice it until something goes wrong or I freeze up. Then I look back and think, “Maybe I was already overloaded,” but in the moment it just feels like I’m trying to get through things.

So… yes and no, I guess. I don’t have a clear answer. I know the blanking out scares me, and the pressure around it makes me feel overwhelmed. Outside of that, I haven’t really paid enough attention to say for sure.
Do you experience memory problems or difficulty recalling information in situations outside of your work?

I’m not sure if it happens as much outside work, or maybe I just don’t notice it the same way because there isn’t someone waiting on me or traffic depending on me. At work it’s very obvious because I’ll be looking right at the road-closure forms, or I’ll have the stop-slow paddle in my hand, and suddenly I can’t remember the steps I’ve done for years. It’s like my mind just goes completely blank at the worst possible time.

Outside work… I mean, I do have moments where I feel like I lose the thread of what I’m doing, but the ones that really scare me are the work ones because they’re so basic to my job. It’s not like I’m learning something new. I know those procedures. I’ve done them over and over, and then suddenly it’s like I can’t access them. That’s the part that made me come in, honestly.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body watching yourself during these blank moments?

I don’t know… I don’t think I’d describe it like being outside my body exactly. Not like I’m up on the ceiling watching myself or anything like that. It’s more that everything sort of stops in my head, and I’m still there, I know I’m there, I know I’m holding the paddle or looking at the paperwork, but I can’t connect to what I’m supposed to do next.

Sometimes afterward I think back on it and it feels kind of unreal, but in the moment I’m mostly just frozen and embarrassed and trying to make myself function. I’m aware of my body, like I can feel myself standing there, and I can hear things going on around me, but it’s like there’s a delay between me and my own thinking.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed the “watching myself from outside” feeling. If anything, it’s more like I’m trapped inside my head while it’s not working properly, if that makes sense.
Do you feel like you're in a daze or disconnected from your surroundings when these blank moments happen?

Kind of, yes, but I don’t know if “disconnected from my surroundings” is exactly the word I’d use. It’s more like my mind just shuts off right in the middle of something I should know how to do. Like I’ll be standing there with the stop-slow paddle, or looking at the road-closure forms, and suddenly I can’t remember the next step. And these are things I’ve done for years, so it’s not like I’m confused because it’s new.

I’m still aware of where I am, like I know I’m at work and I know cars are there and people are expecting me to do what I’m supposed to do. But it feels like I’m in this mental fog, or like there’s nothing available in my head for a few moments. That’s what scares me. It happens at the worst times, when I need my brain to work, and instead it just goes blank.

So maybe “dazed” fits more than disconnected. I don’t feel totally gone, but I feel stuck, like I’m there but I can’t get my thoughts to move.
Do you ever feel like things around you aren't real during these blank moments?

I’m not sure I’d say things around me aren’t real. I don’t think I’ve had that exact feeling, like the cars or the cones or the people around me are fake or like I’m in a dream or something. It’s more that everything is happening and I know it’s happening, but I can’t quite process it fast enough in that moment.

Like, I’ll still recognize where I am. I know I’m at the job site, I know the road is there, I know there are drivers waiting, and I know I’m supposed to be doing something. It doesn’t look unreal to me, exactly. It’s just like my brain stops connecting the pieces together, and then because I’m stuck like that, the whole situation can feel strange afterward when I think about it.

So… no, I don’t think I’d describe it as the world not feeling real. More like I feel foggy and frozen while everything around me keeps going.
Have these blank moments affected your relationships with coworkers or your ability to perform your job overall?

Yes… it’s affected it a lot. More than I wanted to admit for a long time.

At work, I used to be someone people could count on. I mean, I know the job, I’ve done the traffic-safety steps so many times, and I understand how serious it is because if you hesitate or miss something, it’s not just embarrassing, it can be dangerous. But with these blank moments, I stopped trusting myself. I’d get stuck on things like the road-closure paperwork, where I couldn’t finish it or I’d have to stare at it and keep checking because I couldn’t hold the steps in my head. And out on the road, I’d worry, “What if I freeze right when I need to signal or move people through safely?” That kind of fear made me less reliable, and I think other people noticed.

With coworkers, I started pulling back. I didn’t want them to see me mess up or have to cover for me, and I was ashamed, so I’d get quiet or avoid talking more than I had to. I could feel myself becoming someone they couldn’t depend on in the same way, and that hurt because I wasn’t trying to be careless. I just couldn’t make my brain cooperate.

And it didn’t stay only at work. I pulled away from choir and volunteering too, and even from my family. I kept telling myself I just needed to get it together, but I wasn’t really functioning like myself. Eventually my family got worried enough that they felt like they had to bring me in for help, because I wasn’t handling things, not at work and not outside of it either.
Have you noticed any changes in your behavior or how you're functioning in your daily life outside of work since these blank moments started happening?

Yes… outside of work it changed a lot too. I think at first I tried to tell myself it was just stress from the job, or being tired, or that I could sort of contain it there, but it didn’t stay in that box.

I stopped doing things I used to show up for. Choir was one of the first things I pulled back from, because I didn’t trust myself to keep up or even just be present the way I normally would. Volunteering too — I used to care about being dependable, being someone who came when I said I would, but I started canceling or avoiding it because I felt like I couldn’t count on my own mind. It’s embarrassing to say that, because those were things that made me feel useful.

And with my family, I withdrew. I wasn’t talking as much, wasn’t participating like I used to. I think I kept trying to hide how badly I was functioning, but that probably made it more obvious. They could tell I wasn’t myself. I’d get stuck, or overwhelmed, or just not follow through on normal things, and eventually they got worried enough that they felt like they had to bring me in for help.

So yes, it wasn’t just the road-closure paperwork or not trusting myself with the traffic-safety steps at work. It spread into the rest of my life, where I stopped being reliable and started pulling away from almost everyone.
Have you been experiencing feelings of sadness or hopelessness lately?

Yes… yes, I have. It’s been pretty constant lately, especially in the mornings.

Most mornings I wake up and there’s this heavy, hollow sadness sitting in my chest before I’ve even really done anything. It’s like the day already feels ruined before I put my feet on the floor. I’ll open my eyes and for a second I’m just lying there, and instead of feeling like, okay, I need to get up and start the day, it’s more like this sinking feeling, like I already don’t have enough in me for whatever the day is going to ask from me.

And it’s not just regular being tired or having a bad mood, at least it doesn’t feel that way. It feels deeper than that, like something is weighing me down from the inside. I don’t always have a clear reason for it right when I wake up, which almost makes it worse, because then I start thinking, “Why do I feel this awful already?” But it’s there before anything even happens.

Hopelessness… I guess that’s part of it too. Not every second, but when I wake up feeling like that, it’s hard not to feel like nothing is going to get better that day. It’s like I’m starting from behind before the day even begins.
How long have you been waking up with this heavy, hollow sadness?

It’s been… about a year and two months, I think. Around that long where waking up already feeling heavy and empty became more normal than not.

It wasn’t like one single morning where I thought, “This is the start of something.” It kind of settled in and then stayed. But looking back, the heavy depression, the guilt, the low energy, and not really having much appetite… that whole pattern has been with me for about a year and two months now. Some days are a little different in intensity, but that morning sadness has been there for a long time.
Does the heavy, hollow sadness you feel in the mornings tend to stay with you throughout the day or does it change?

It usually starts right when I wake up, before anything has even happened, and that’s the part that makes it feel so… unfair, I guess. Like I’ll open my eyes and there’s already this heavy, hollow sadness in my chest, and my first thought isn’t even a thought exactly — it’s more like this feeling that the day is already ruined before I’ve even put my feet on the floor.

As the day goes on, it can shift a little. Sometimes I can get distracted for a while or go through the motions, but it doesn’t feel like it completely leaves. It’s more like it’s sitting underneath everything. The morning is usually when it feels the most obvious and crushing, because there’s nothing to blame it on yet. I haven’t done anything wrong, nothing has happened, but I already feel like I’m starting the day buried under it.

So… it changes in intensity, I guess, but that heaviness tends to follow me. It’s not like I wake up sad and then by lunch I’m suddenly fine. It’s there in the background, and sometimes it comes back up really strong again if I stop and notice it.
Have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy since these blank moments and feelings of sadness started?

Yes… I have. A lot, actually.

I used to be the person who was always in the middle of things, not in a loud way maybe, but dependable. Like with choir, I’d be the one figuring out rides, texting people, making sure somebody’s kid wasn’t left without a way there. Or with the garden swaps, I’d be asking who had extra seedlings, who needed jars, who was bringing what. And youth basketball snacks too — I used to keep track of whose turn it was, remind the other parents, sometimes just do it myself if somebody forgot.

And now it’s like… I see the messages come in, and I just don’t feel that push in me to answer. I can sit there for hours with my phone right next to me, or even in my hand, staring at the screen, and I know I should reply. I know people are probably waiting on me. But there’s this blankness, like the part of me that used to care enough to jump up and organize things is just not connecting.

It’s not that I suddenly hate those things or those people. That’s what makes me feel bad about it. I remember enjoying being useful and involved. I remember feeling like, okay, this is where I fit. But lately it feels far away, like something I used to do because I was a different version of myself. Now I just sit there and let the phone light up, and I don’t answer.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight lately?

Yeah… I think so. I don’t weigh myself regularly, so I can’t give you an exact number, but I’ve noticed it in my clothes. My flagger pants — the ones I wear for work — they’ve been sitting looser on me, like I keep having to pull them up or adjust them more than I used to. At first I thought maybe they’d stretched out or something, but then other clothes started feeling kind of the same.

Food just… doesn’t mean much to me lately. I don’t really think about it the way I used to. I’ll realize it’s late in the day and I haven’t eaten, not because I was trying not to, just because it didn’t occur to me or nothing sounded worth the effort. Sometimes my family will ask if I ate, or they’ll say I look drawn, like my face looks thinner or tired or something, and that makes me feel embarrassed because I didn’t really notice it happening.

So yes, I think I’ve lost weight. I just don’t know how much.
Do you ever find yourself doing something or being somewhere without remembering how you got there after one of these blank moments?

Not exactly like I wake up somewhere and have no idea how I got there… I don’t think it’s been that dramatic. But I do have these moments where my mind just goes blank right in the middle of something I should absolutely know how to do.

That’s actually a big reason I came in. It scares me because it happens at the worst times. Like I’ll be looking at the road-closure forms, or I’ll have the stop-slow paddle in my hand, and suddenly it’s like the steps are gone. These are things I’ve done for years — not complicated new things, not something someone just trained me on yesterday — but in that moment I can’t remember what comes next, or I’m staring at the page and it’s like the words are there but my brain won’t grab onto them.

It feels less like I went somewhere and forgot the trip, and more like I’m standing right there, but the part of me that knows what to do just shuts off. And then I get panicky because I know I should know. I’ll think, “Come on, you know this, you’ve done this a thousand times,” but that almost makes it worse because then I’m aware I’m blanking and I can’t force it back fast enough.

So… no, I don’t think I’ve found myself in a place without remembering how I arrived. But I do lose the thread badly enough that I feel like I can’t trust my own mind sometimes, especially with work stuff where there are steps I’m supposed to follow.
Do you still find pleasure in the things you used to enjoy before these blank moments and feelings of sadness started?

Not really… no. I keep trying to tell myself maybe if I just show up, it’ll come back, but it doesn’t feel the same.

Like I said, I used to really get something out of being involved. Choir rides, for example — I wasn’t just doing logistics. I liked knowing people could count on me, that everybody would get there, that I was part of the group. Same with the garden swaps. I used to enjoy the little back-and-forth messages about who had tomato starts or extra jars or who needed help carrying things. Even youth basketball snacks, which sounds silly, but I liked keeping track of it. I liked being useful.

Now my phone will light up with those same kinds of messages, and I’ll just… stare at it. Sometimes for hours. I can see someone asking a normal question, something I would have answered right away before, and there’s just no push in me. No spark, I guess. I don’t feel that little tug of interest or satisfaction. It’s like I know those things mattered to me, but I can’t feel the mattering in the moment.

And then I feel guilty, because these are good people and I haven’t stopped caring about them exactly. It’s more like the part of me that used to enjoy joining in and organizing things has gone quiet. I miss that version of myself, honestly.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in most activities nearly every day?

Yes. Yeah, definitely at least two weeks… honestly it feels like it’s been more than that, but I know you’re asking about that kind of stretch where it’s almost every day, and yes.

Most mornings I wake up and there’s this heavy, hollow sadness sitting in my chest before anything has even happened. Like I haven’t checked my phone, I haven’t gone outside, nobody’s said anything to me yet, and somehow the day already feels ruined. I’ll just lie there for a minute thinking, “I have to do this whole day?” and it feels like too much before I even put my feet on the floor.

It’s not just a bad mood that passes once I get moving, either. I keep hoping maybe if I start doing normal things, it’ll lift, but that heaviness is there most days. Some mornings are worse than others, but it’s been there enough that I can’t really pretend it’s just one rough week or one bad weekend. It’s like I wake up already behind, already sad, already empty.

Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you either felt depressed or lost interest in most activities nearly every day, and also experienced at least several other symptoms like changes in appetite or sleep?

Yes… yes, I have. It’s not just two weeks, though. I wish it were something that short and neat, like I could point to a rough couple of weeks and say, “That was the bad patch.”

The heavy depression has been with me for about a year and two months now. Around that long. It’s been this constant weight — not every single minute at the exact same level, but nearly every day there’s something there. The sadness, the guilt, the low energy… and I’ve had a loss of appetite with it too. It all kind of runs together after a while, which makes it hard to explain without sounding like I’m exaggerating, but I’m not.

It’s like I’ve been dragging myself through the days for over a year, and I keep thinking I should be able to shake it off or get back to myself, but it hasn’t lifted. The guilt is there a lot too, like I’m failing at things I used to handle, and then I don’t have the energy to fix them, and then I feel worse. And eating… I just don’t feel much pull toward food the way I used to. Sometimes it feels like one more thing I’m supposed to make myself do.

So, yes — definitely more than two weeks. More like about a year and two months of this.

Yes… it’s affected it a lot. More than I wanted to admit for a long time.

At work, I used to be someone people could count on. I mean, I know the job, I’ve done the traffic-safety steps so many times, and I understand how serious it is because if you hesitate or miss something, it’s not just embarrassing, it can be dangerous. But with these blank moments, I stopped trusting myself. I’d get stuck on things like the road-closure paperwork, where I couldn’t finish it or I’d have to stare at it and keep checking because I couldn’t hold the steps in my head. And out on the road, I’d worry, “What if I freeze right when I need to signal or move people through safely?” That kind of fear made me less reliable, and I think other people noticed.

With coworkers, I started pulling back. I didn’t want them to see me mess up or have to cover for me, and I was ashamed, so I’d get quiet or avoid talking more than I had to. I could feel myself becoming someone they couldn’t depend on in the same way, and that hurt because I wasn’t trying to be careless. I just couldn’t make my brain cooperate.

And it didn’t stay only at work. I pulled away from choir and volunteering too, and even from my family. I kept telling myself I just needed to get it together, but I wasn’t really functioning like myself. Eventually my family got worried enough that they felt like they had to bring me in for help, because I wasn’t handling things, not at work and not outside of it either.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of a significant change in the patient's behavior or functioning outside of work due to the blank moments
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your behavior or how you're functioning in your daily life outside of work since these blank moments started happening?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I stopped being reliable at work because I could not finish road-closure paperwork or trust myself with traffic-safety steps, and I pulled away from choir, volunteering, and family until they felt they had to bring me for help.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in daily-life functioning and behavior outside work, which is most directly about overall functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… outside of work it changed a lot too. I think at first I tried to tell myself it was just stress from the job, or being tired, or that I could sort of contain it there, but it didn’t stay in that box.

I stopped doing things I used to show up for. Choir was one of the first things I pulled back from, because I didn’t trust myself to keep up or even just be present the way I normally would. Volunteering too — I used to care about being dependable, being someone who came when I said I would, but I started canceling or avoiding it because I felt like I couldn’t count on my own mind. It’s embarrassing to say that, because those were things that made me feel useful.

And with my family, I withdrew. I wasn’t talking as much, wasn’t participating like I used to. I think I kept trying to hide how badly I was functioning, but that probably made it more obvious. They could tell I wasn’t myself. I’d get stuck, or overwhelmed, or just not follow through on normal things, and eventually they got worried enough that they felt like they had to bring me in for help.

So yes, it wasn’t just the road-closure paperwork or not trusting myself with the traffic-safety steps at work. It spread into the rest of my life, where I stopped being reliable and started pulling away from almost everyone.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Have you been experiencing feelings of sadness or hopelessness lately?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow sadness in my chest, like the day is already ruined before I even put my feet on the floor.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about sadness and hopelessness, which matches depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I have. It’s been pretty constant lately, especially in the mornings.

Most mornings I wake up and there’s this heavy, hollow sadness sitting in my chest before I’ve even really done anything. It’s like the day already feels ruined before I put my feet on the floor. I’ll open my eyes and for a second I’m just lying there, and instead of feeling like, okay, I need to get up and start the day, it’s more like this sinking feeling, like I already don’t have enough in me for whatever the day is going to ask from me.

And it’s not just regular being tired or having a bad mood, at least it doesn’t feel that way. It feels deeper than that, like something is weighing me down from the inside. I don’t always have a clear reason for it right when I wake up, which almost makes it worse, because then I start thinking, “Why do I feel this awful already?” But it’s there before anything even happens.

Hopelessness… I guess that’s part of it too. Not every second, but when I wake up feeling like that, it’s hard not to feel like nothing is going to get better that day. It’s like I’m starting from behind before the day even begins.

inference.note: Added F32.0 and F32.1 due to reported feelings of sadness and hopelessness, ruled out R41.0 and G31.84 as primary concerns

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the patient's feelings of sadness or hopelessness
doctor.question: How long have you been waking up with this heavy, hollow sadness?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The heavy depression, guilt, low energy, and loss of appetite have been with me for about a year and two months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the heavy, hollow sadness has been occurring, which directly matches the duration of the depressive episode.

patient.answer:
It’s been… about a year and two months, I think. Around that long where waking up already feeling heavy and empty became more normal than not.

It wasn’t like one single morning where I thought, “This is the start of something.” It kind of settled in and then stayed. But looking back, the heavy depression, the guilt, the low energy, and not really having much appetite… that whole pattern has been with me for about a year and two months now. Some days are a little different in intensity, but that morning sadness has been there for a long time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's sadness is persistent throughout the day or if it varies
doctor.question: Does the heavy, hollow sadness you feel in the mornings tend to stay with you throughout the day or does it change?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow sadness in my chest, like the day is already ruined before I even put my feet on the floor.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the morning heavy, hollow sadness persists through the day or changes, which directly concerns depressed mood.

patient.answer:
It usually starts right when I wake up, before anything has even happened, and that’s the part that makes it feel so… unfair, I guess. Like I’ll open my eyes and there’s already this heavy, hollow sadness in my chest, and my first thought isn’t even a thought exactly — it’s more like this feeling that the day is already ruined before I’ve even put my feet on the floor.

As the day goes on, it can shift a little. Sometimes I can get distracted for a while or go through the motions, but it doesn’t feel like it completely leaves. It’s more like it’s sitting underneath everything. The morning is usually when it feels the most obvious and crushing, because there’s nothing to blame it on yet. I haven’t done anything wrong, nothing has happened, but I already feel like I’m starting the day buried under it.

So… it changes in intensity, I guess, but that heaviness tends to follow me. It’s not like I wake up sad and then by lunch I’m suddenly fine. It’s there in the background, and sometimes it comes back up really strong again if I stop and notice it.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy since these blank moments and feelings of sadness started?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I used to be the one organizing choir rides, garden swaps, and youth basketball snacks, but now I can sit for hours staring at my phone and not feel the push to answer anybody.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, which matches diminished motivation and social interest.

patient.answer:
Yes… I have. A lot, actually.

I used to be the person who was always in the middle of things, not in a loud way maybe, but dependable. Like with choir, I’d be the one figuring out rides, texting people, making sure somebody’s kid wasn’t left without a way there. Or with the garden swaps, I’d be asking who had extra seedlings, who needed jars, who was bringing what. And youth basketball snacks too — I used to keep track of whose turn it was, remind the other parents, sometimes just do it myself if somebody forgot.

And now it’s like… I see the messages come in, and I just don’t feel that push in me to answer. I can sit there for hours with my phone right next to me, or even in my hand, staring at the screen, and I know I should reply. I know people are probably waiting on me. But there’s this blankness, like the part of me that used to care enough to jump up and organize things is just not connecting.

It’s not that I suddenly hate those things or those people. That’s what makes me feel bad about it. I remember enjoying being useful and involved. I remember feeling like, okay, this is where I fit. But lately it feels far away, like something I used to do because I was a different version of myself. Now I just sit there and let the phone light up, and I don’t answer.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight lately?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: Food has stopped meaning much to me, and I skip meals without noticing until my flagger pants are loose and my family starts asking why I look so drawn.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about significant changes in weight lately, which matches the weight/appetite change symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I don’t weigh myself regularly, so I can’t give you an exact number, but I’ve noticed it in my clothes. My flagger pants — the ones I wear for work — they’ve been sitting looser on me, like I keep having to pull them up or adjust them more than I used to. At first I thought maybe they’d stretched out or something, but then other clothes started feeling kind of the same.

Food just… doesn’t mean much to me lately. I don’t really think about it the way I used to. I’ll realize it’s late in the day and I haven’t eaten, not because I was trying not to, just because it didn’t occur to me or nothing sounded worth the effort. Sometimes my family will ask if I ate, or they’ll say I look drawn, like my face looks thinner or tired or something, and that makes me feel embarrassed because I didn’t really notice it happening.

So yes, I think I’ve lost weight. I just don’t know how much.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's blank moments are accompanied by a loss of consciousness or awareness of their surroundings
doctor.question: Do you ever find yourself doing something or being somewhere without remembering how you got there after one of these blank moments?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: I came in because my mind keeps going blank at the worst times, like I will look at the road-closure forms or the stop-slow paddle and suddenly cannot remember the steps I have done for years.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the patient’s blank moments and whether they involve memory or awareness gaps, which is most directly related to diminished thinking/concentration.

patient.answer:
Not exactly like I wake up somewhere and have no idea how I got there… I don’t think it’s been that dramatic. But I do have these moments where my mind just goes blank right in the middle of something I should absolutely know how to do.

That’s actually a big reason I came in. It scares me because it happens at the worst times. Like I’ll be looking at the road-closure forms, or I’ll have the stop-slow paddle in my hand, and suddenly it’s like the steps are gone. These are things I’ve done for years — not complicated new things, not something someone just trained me on yesterday — but in that moment I can’t remember what comes next, or I’m staring at the page and it’s like the words are there but my brain won’t grab onto them.

It feels less like I went somewhere and forgot the trip, and more like I’m standing right there, but the part of me that knows what to do just shuts off. And then I get panicky because I know I should know. I’ll think, “Come on, you know this, you’ve done this a thousand times,” but that almost makes it worse because then I’m aware I’m blanking and I can’t force it back fast enough.

So… no, I don’t think I’ve found myself in a place without remembering how I arrived. But I do lose the thread badly enough that I feel like I can’t trust my own mind sometimes, especially with work stuff where there are steps I’m supposed to follow.

doctor.question: Do you still find pleasure in the things you used to enjoy before these blank moments and feelings of sadness started?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I used to be the one organizing choir rides, garden swaps, and youth basketball snacks, but now I can sit for hours staring at my phone and not feel the push to answer anybody.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about loss of pleasure or interest in previously enjoyed activities, which is most directly reflected by diminished motivation and social interest.

patient.answer:
Not really… no. I keep trying to tell myself maybe if I just show up, it’ll come back, but it doesn’t feel the same.

Like I said, I used to really get something out of being involved. Choir rides, for example — I wasn’t just doing logistics. I liked knowing people could count on me, that everybody would get there, that I was part of the group. Same with the garden swaps. I used to enjoy the little back-and-forth messages about who had tomato starts or extra jars or who needed help carrying things. Even youth basketball snacks, which sounds silly, but I liked keeping track of it. I liked being useful.

Now my phone will light up with those same kinds of messages, and I’ll just… stare at it. Sometimes for hours. I can see someone asking a normal question, something I would have answered right away before, and there’s just no push in me. No spark, I guess. I don’t feel that little tug of interest or satisfaction. It’s like I know those things mattered to me, but I can’t feel the mattering in the moment.

And then I feel guilty, because these are good people and I haven’t stopped caring about them exactly. It’s more like the part of me that used to enjoy joining in and organizing things has gone quiet. I miss that version of myself, honestly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in most activities nearly every day?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow sadness in my chest, like the day is already ruined before I even put my feet on the floor.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether a depressed mood or loss of interest persisted nearly every day for at least two weeks, which is most directly captured by the depressed mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Yes. Yeah, definitely at least two weeks… honestly it feels like it’s been more than that, but I know you’re asking about that kind of stretch where it’s almost every day, and yes.

Most mornings I wake up and there’s this heavy, hollow sadness sitting in my chest before anything has even happened. Like I haven’t checked my phone, I haven’t gone outside, nobody’s said anything to me yet, and somehow the day already feels ruined. I’ll just lie there for a minute thinking, “I have to do this whole day?” and it feels like too much before I even put my feet on the floor.

It’s not just a bad mood that passes once I get moving, either. I keep hoping maybe if I start doing normal things, it’ll lift, but that heaviness is there most days. Some mornings are worse than others, but it’s been there enough that I can’t really pretend it’s just one rough week or one bad weekend. It’s like I wake up already behind, already sad, already empty.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you had a period of at least two weeks where you either felt depressed or lost interest in most activities nearly every day, and also experienced at least several other symptoms like changes in appetite or sleep?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The heavy depression, guilt, low energy, and loss of appetite have been with me for about a year and two months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether there has been a depressive episode lasting at least two weeks with depressed mood or loss of interest plus other depressive symptoms; this item directly covers the duration and symptom cluster of the depressive episode.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I have. It’s not just two weeks, though. I wish it were something that short and neat, like I could point to a rough couple of weeks and say, “That was the bad patch.”

The heavy depression has been with me for about a year and two months now. Around that long. It’s been this constant weight — not every single minute at the exact same level, but nearly every day there’s something there. The sadness, the guilt, the low energy… and I’ve had a loss of appetite with it too. It all kind of runs together after a while, which makes it hard to explain without sounding like I’m exaggerating, but I’m not.

It’s like I’ve been dragging myself through the days for over a year, and I keep thinking I should be able to shake it off or get back to myself, but it hasn’t lifted. The guilt is there a lot too, like I’m failing at things I used to handle, and then I don’t have the energy to fix them, and then I feel worse. And eating… I just don’t feel much pull toward food the way I used to. Sometimes it feels like one more thing I’m supposed to make myself do.

So, yes — definitely more than two weeks. More like about a year and two months of this.

inference.note: F43.8 was ruled out as the patient's symptoms align more closely with depressive disorders, and the presence of persistent sadness, loss of interest, and changes in appetite and sleep patterns support this diagnosis
